problem: Image-goal navigation in a novel, never-seen environment requires both exploration and memory. Prior approaches either assume prior experience of the environment (demonstrations, pre-built topological maps as in SPTM, or per-environment RL training) or use metrically precise maps. Those metric maps scale poorly and become inconsistent under realistic actuation and odometry noise. End-to-end RL policies also struggle to learn structural and semantic priors for exploration, especially when an explicit STOP action is required.
motivation: Humans navigate a new house using coarse topological layouts and semantic priors (an oven is likely reached through the kitchen doorway), not exact metric maps. The paper argues that two ingredients are needed: a spatial representation robust to pose noise, and explicit modeling of structural and semantic priors. It also argues that learning everything via RL with poor credit assignment is sample-inefficient, whereas every needed function can be learned by supervised learning from automatically labeled image pairs.
key_idea: Build an online topological graph whose nodes are panoramic images linked by coarse relative poses, expand it with learned 'ghost' nodes in predicted explorable directions, and rank those ghost nodes with a learned goal-conditioned semantic score. All four required functions (localization, explorable area, semantic score, relative pose) are learned by one supervised multi-task network.
insight: Storing only relative poses between consecutive nodes, a few actions apart, keeps odometry error from accumulating. Table 2 (no-noise) supports this: metric-map baselines gain substantially when noise is removed (ANS overall SR 0.44→0.54, hard 0.16→0.30), while NTS barely changes (0.63→0.64); NTS's margin is also largest on Hard episodes (0.43 vs 0.16 SR, RGBD). The learned semantic score F_S encodes structural priors. In the sequential-goal ablation (Fig. 8), removing F_S (random ghost-node choice) hurts most on the first goal, while removing the graph (greedy direction choice, no memory) hurts increasingly as more goals are chained; this shows semantics matter early and memory matters over time. RL baselines are especially hurt by the explicit STOP action: Target-driven RL rises from 0.33 to 0.52 SR without STOP. This suggests supervised learning of decomposed functions avoids a hard exploration and credit-assignment problem.
method: Topological map: graph of regular nodes (each a 360° panorama representing its visible area, radius r=3m); edges store relative pose Δp estimated from noisy odometry between consecutive nodes. 'Ghost' nodes mark unexplored directions and carry the image patch in that direction.

Graph Update: the Graph Localization function F_L tries to localize the current panorama in an existing node. If it lands in a different node, the agent moves there and an edge is added. If not localized, a new node plus an edge to the last node (with odometry Δp) is created. Ghost nodes are added at (r=3m, θ) for each of 12 directions that F_G predicts as explorable, and they are removed or suppressed where a regular node already lies in that direction.

Global Policy: localize the goal image in the graph with F_L. If localized, that node is the long-term goal; otherwise F_S scores all ghost nodes for proximity to the goal and the highest-scoring one is chosen. Dijkstra on the graph gives the next subgoal node, and its edge Δp is passed down. Once in the goal's node, F_R predicts the goal's relative pose.

Local Policy: a PointGoal policy adapted from Active Neural SLAM. It builds a local spatial map (learned mapper for RGB, geometric depth projection for RGB-D) and plans a shortest path to the relative goal, issuing forward 25cm / turn ±10° / stop actions.

NTS multi-task model: each 128×512 panorama is split into 12 overlapping 128×128 patches. Patches go through a shared ResNet18 encoder (RGB-D adds a separate non-pretrained ResNet18 branch for depth) to 128-d patch features. A Connection head predicts same-node or not (F_L). An Intra-node head predicts the 30° direction bin and a distance score (F_R). An Inter-node head predicts per-direction explorability (F_G) and per-direction semantic score toward the goal (F_S).
Training: cross-entropy for connection and direction labels, MSE for score labels (weight 10); Adam, lr 5e-4, batch 64; trained fully offline with no environment interaction.

Automated labeling from GT training maps: connection = goal visible within a 5° depth patch and within 3m; intra-node score s = max(1 − d/r, 0); inter-node direction label = 1 if the geodesic path to the point at 3m is < 1.05r; inter-node score s_i = max(1 − d_i/20m, 0), where d_i is the geodesic distance from the farthest traversable point in direction i to the goal.

setting.backbone: NTS multi-task net: shared ResNet18 patch encoder + FC heads (trained with supervision); Local Policy from Active Neural SLAM (learned mapper for RGB / depth projection for RGB-D + shortest-path planner)
setting.training_data: Gibson (Habitat curated 86 scenes split 68/4/14 train/val/test): 300 random panoramic images per training scene, all ordered pairs auto-labeled from GT maps ≈ 6.12M pairs (68×300×300); offline supervised, no RL or environment interaction
setting.observation: panoramic RGB or RGB-D (128×512) + noisy odometry pose sensor (Δx, Δy, Δθ); goal is a panoramic image
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: FORWARD ~25cm, TURN LEFT/RIGHT ~10°, STOP, with realistic actuation noise (continuous state space)
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT maps only used to generate training labels; test scenes need no sampling or GT map)

numbers_note: All metrics are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.63); they are converted here to 0-100. The benchmark is NTS's own panoramic Gibson image-goal episode set (14 test scenes of a 68/4/14 split), so it is not directly comparable to the standard Habitat Gibson ImageNav (non-panoramic) numbers. The sequential-goal ablations (NTS w/o Graph, NTS w/o Score Function, 1-5 sequential goals) are reported only in Figure 8, with no numeric values.
results: On panoramic image-goal navigation in unseen Gibson scenes with realistic noise, NTS reaches overall SR/SPL 0.63/0.43 (RGBD) and 0.55/0.38 (RGB). The strongest baseline, Active Neural SLAM, gets 0.44/0.29 and 0.35/0.23 respectively, a >50% relative improvement in RGB. The gap grows with difficulty (Hard RGBD 0.43/0.26 vs 0.16/0.09). NTS also beats Metric Map + FBE, Metric Map + RL, Target-driven RL and ResNet+GRU+IL, while training offline on fewer samples than the 25M-frame RL baselines. Without noise, NTS barely changes (0.64) while metric-map methods improve markedly, indicating its robustness to pose error.
limitations: Requires 360° panoramic observations and panoramic goal images, and is evaluated on a custom episode set; results are simulation-only (real-robot deployment left as future work).

Training labels depend on ground-truth maps and geodesic distances in training scenes. Node radius (3m) and the 12 discrete directions are fixed hand-set design choices; graph localization compares the query against every node.
Performance drops as sequential goals accumulate (Fig. 8). Ghost nodes carry only a direction at a fixed radius, not predicted positions.
